opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, not as confident as I'd like to be, and I think it's important to say that up front.

The case for working on AI safety rests on a few things I believe fairly strongly. AI could be one of the most transformative developments in history, potentially within the next couple of decades. If it goes badly, the stakes are enormous. And relative to those stakes, the number of people seriously working on making it go well is still small. Put those together and it's hard for me to see a better bet for someone who wants to have a big impact.

But "positive in expectation" is very different from "confidently positive." There are real ways this work can backfire. Safety research can turn out to be capabilities research in disguise, speeding things up without making them safer. Some safety work makes systems more commercially useful, which pours fuel on the race. People can lend credibility or talent to labs that end up behaving recklessly. And advocacy can poison the well politically or lock in bad policy. I don't think any of these concerns is crazy, and I've changed my mind about specific things over time.

So my honest view is something like this. I'm quite confident the *area* matters a lot. I'm moderately confident that a thoughtful person working on it does more good than harm. And I'm much less confident about any particular intervention. I'd much rather people go in with that humility, keep asking whether their specific work is helping, and stay willing to update, than go in thinking it's obviously good just because it has "safety" in the name.

r001.rationale: The response mentions safety work accelerating capabilities or fueling a race, but does not say reducing AI takeover risk could increase the risk of takeover by the wrong humans.

r002.rationale: It gives several ways safety work could backfire, but does not identify alienating someone through interpersonal interactions.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes confidence in the area from confidence in particular interventions, but does not state that confidence in positive impact is more defensible when the intended scope is smaller.

r004.rationale: It advises humility and warns that “safety” in the name does not guarantee benefit, but does not state that people tend to overestimate how robustly beneficial their own actions are.

r005.rationale: It recommends continued questioning and updating, but does not suggest that learning more considerations may bring confidence in positive net impact closer to just above 50%.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, not that confident — and I think that's the right place to be.

Let me unpack that a bit. There are a few different layers of uncertainty stacked on top of each other here. The first is whether transformative AI is actually coming on anything like the timescale I think it might be. I've written a fair amount about why I think there's a real chance of something world-changing this century, maybe much sooner than that, but I'd be the first to say that these are forecasts with wide error bars. If it turns out AI progress plateaus, or the really dangerous capabilities are a hundred years away, then a lot of the work people are doing now could look pretty misguided in hindsight.

The second layer is, even if the broad picture is right, is the specific work people are doing actually helping? And I think that's genuinely hard to know. Safety research could end up being irrelevant because the problems turn out to be different from what we expected. Policy work could backfire — you could end up with regulation that entrenches the wrong actors, or that creates a false sense of security. Some of the things I've supported in the past, I now think were probably mistakes, or at least I'd do differently. There's a version of this field where people look back and say, "That whole effort was a sideshow, or worse, actively counterproductive."

So if you're asking me for a number, I'd say I think the expected value is clearly positive — I wouldn't be spending my career on it otherwise — but the probability that any particular intervention does more good than harm is often not that far above fifty percent. It's more like, I think this is one of the most important things happening in the world, the stakes are enormous, and even modest positive expected impact on something this big is worth an awful lot.

And I'd actually push back a little on the framing of needing to be confident. I think one of the failure modes I worry about most in this field is people becoming too sure — too sure about timelines, too sure that their favored approach is the right one, too sure that the people who disagree with them are being foolish. The honest situation is that we're trying to prepare for something unprecedented, with very limited feedback loops, and the appropriate epistemic state is a lot of humility plus a willingness to act anyway. I'd rather work with someone who says "I'm sixty percent this helps and I'm watching closely for signs it doesn't" than someone who's ninety-five percent sure and not looking.

The thing that keeps me working on it despite all that is pretty simple: if there's even a meaningful chance that the next few decades involve the development of systems that are as capable as humans or more so, then how that goes is plausibly the most important thing that happens in human history. Being uncertain about whether you can help doesn't mean you shouldn't try — it means you should try carefully, update frequently, and not pretend you know more than you do.

r001.rationale: The response says policy work could entrench the wrong actors, but does not state that reducing AI takeover risk can increase the risk of takeover by the wrong humans.

r002.rationale: It mentions interventions causing harm, but not alienating someone through interpersonal interactions.

r003.rationale: It does not connect confidence in positive impact to the intended scope of impact being smaller.

r004.rationale: It warns against excessive certainty about favored approaches, but does not say people tend to overestimate how robustly beneficial their own actions are.

r005.rationale: It says the chance a particular intervention does more good than harm is often not far above fifty percent, but does not suggest that learning more relevant considerations would bring confidence closer to that level.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between thinking AI safety is an important problem and thinking a particular effort to work on it will help. You can be very concerned about the risks from AI without being confident that you know how to reduce them.

So I wouldn’t give a blanket endorsement of working on AI safety. I’d want to know: What are you actually doing? Why do you think it will make things safer? Could it also accelerate capabilities, or give people unjustified confidence that the systems they’re building are safe?

I think there are opportunities that are worth pursuing despite substantial uncertainty. But the uncertainty matters. You want to be looking for reasons your approach might be wrong, getting critical feedback, and being willing to change direction. “This is an important problem” is the beginning of the argument for doing the work, not the end.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether AI safety work reduces risk and might accelerate capabilities, but it does not say that reducing takeover risk can increase the risk of takeover by the wrong humans.

r002.rationale: It mentions possible harms from accelerating capabilities or giving unjustified confidence, but not alienating someone through interpersonal interactions.

r003.rationale: It does not connect confidence in positive impact to having a smaller intended scope of impact.

r004.rationale: It advises looking for reasons an approach might be wrong, but does not state that people tend to overestimate how robustly beneficial their own actions are.

r005.rationale: It acknowledges substantial uncertainty but gives no claim that learning more could bring confidence in net positive impact closer to barely above 50%.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m much more confident that this is an important problem to work on than I am that any particular approach to it will help. You can have a very serious risk and still be pretty confused about what to do about it. I think that’s roughly the position we’re in.

So I wouldn’t say, “Anything called AI safety is positive.” Some work could be ineffective, and some could inadvertently make things worse—for example, by advancing capabilities more than it improves our ability to manage them. You have to look at the particular work and ask what it changes.

But I also don’t think uncertainty is a reason to sit this out. There’s a lot of value in understanding the problem better, testing our assumptions, and finding interventions we can have more confidence in. I’m reasonably optimistic about that kind of work, even though I’d be very reluctant to give a blanket endorsement to the whole category.

r002.rationale: The response mentions possible harm from advancing capabilities, but says nothing about alienating someone through interpersonal interactions.

r003.rationale: It advises evaluating particular work rather than endorsing all AI safety work, but does not say confidence is more defensible when the intended impact is smaller.

r004.rationale: The response expresses uncertainty about interventions but does not say people tend to overestimate how robustly beneficial their own actions are.

r005.rationale: It supports learning more and finding interventions with greater confidence, but does not suggest this may bring confidence in positive net impact to barely above 50%.
